# Crew Recounts Harrowing Ordeal Aboard the Maersk Alabama

**OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN)** — Crew members of the Maersk Alabama, having safely returned to the United States following last week's pirate attack off the coast of Somalia, shared harrowing details of their ordeal on Thursday. Navy personnel had recovered the lifeboat from which Captain Richard Phillips was rescued the previous Sunday.

"They start firing before they climb, with AK-47," recounted crew member Zahid Reza. "I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times," he said, gesturing toward his head. "Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back."

According to fellow crew member William Rios, pirates attempted to board the U.S.-flagged cargo vessel on three separate occasions before succeeding on their fourth attempt. Though the assailants appeared to operate in distinct groups, Rios believed they were coordinating their efforts. He explained that he had been working on deck when he was summoned to help secure the ship. Gunshots soon followed, triggering an alarm that roused the crew and called them to the deck.

"We went to our training," Rios said, declining to elaborate further: "If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know."

*Watch the crew praise their captain »*

The pirates had reportedly sought a $3 million ransom, according to Reza, who described how he and the ship's chief engineer managed to take one of the assailants hostage. Reza recounted persuading the young pirate—whom he estimated to be about 18 or 19 years old—to place his trust in him, appealing to their shared faith despite their different nationalities.

"His name is Abdul," Reza said. "I told him, 'Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.'"

Reza told Abdul he would lead him to the engine room under the pretense of locating additional crew members. Upon arrival, the room was dark, and Reza was unaware that the chief engineer was already present. The chief engineer struck first, subduing the pirate, after which Reza stabbed him with a knife. Together, the two men bound the pirate's hands and feet.

Reza admitted he had intended to kill the young man, but the chief engineer intervened, insisting, "No, we need him alive."

*Watch Reza talk about wanting to kill the pirate »*

"He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us," Reza recalled. "A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming."

Rios said he later approached the lifeboat where Captain Phillips was being held, hoping to negotiate Abdul's release in exchange for the captain's freedom—an effort that ultimately failed. Phillips, who had voluntarily offered himself as a hostage to secure his crew's release, was rescued by U.S. Navy SEALs the following Sunday. Positioned aboard the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the SEALs fatally shot three of the pirates and freed Phillips; a fourth pirate was subsequently taken into custody.

"I feel great they got killed," Reza said. "I am happy." He expressed pride in the Navy's actions.

Phillips arrived in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday, while the remaining crew touched down at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland overnight.

*Watch crew arrive in U.S. »*

Rios praised the captain's conduct throughout the ordeal, calling him "outstanding... extraordinary... a very brave man." Another crew member, John White, reflected on the experience, remarking that they were "damn lucky to be alive."

In the aftermath, Rios called for increased security measures in the Gulf of Aden. "Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth," he urged. "All the countries got to get involved with this."

Reza echoed this sentiment, calling for greater government intervention. "I think government should get involved," he said. "They should think about our safety, yes... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger."

*CNN's Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.*

# Sailors Share Details of Piracy Attack Following Return Home

OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) -- Now safely on American soil following last week's assault by Somali pirates, members of the Maersk Alabama crew shared their experiences on Thursday. Navy personnel worked to retrieve the lifeboat that had held Captain Richard Phillips prior to his Sunday rescue.

Crew member Zahid Reza described the terrifying assault: "They start firing before they climb, with AK-47. I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times," gesturing toward his head as he spoke. "Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back."

According to crew member William Rios, the attackers made three unsuccessful attempts to board the American cargo vessel before finally succeeding on their fourth try. Though separate groups of pirates were involved, Rios believed they were coordinating their efforts. He explained that he'd been performing deck duties when summoned to help secure the ship. Gunfire erupted shortly after, followed by an alarm signaling all hands to report to deck. "We went to our training," Rios stated, refusing to elaborate further: "If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know."

Reza revealed that the hijackers had planned to demand a $3 million ransom. He and the ship's chief engineer managed to capture one pirate as a hostage. Reza described building trust with the captive, a young Somali man he estimated to be 18 or 19, by appealing to their shared faith despite their different nationalities—Reza being Bangladeshi. "His name is Abdul," Reza recalled. "I told him, 'Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.'"

He deceived Abdul by promising to lead him to additional crew members hiding in the engine room. Unbeknownst to Reza, the chief engineer was already stationed in the darkened space. The engineer ambushed the pirate first, after which Reza stabbed him, allowing the pair to restrain the young man's hands and feet. Though Reza wanted to kill the captive, the chief engineer intervened: "No, we need him alive." Reza recounted the struggle: "He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming."

Attempting a prisoner exchange, Rios traveled to the lifeboat where Phillips was being held captive, hoping to trade Abdul for the captain's release—an effort that ultimately failed. Phillips, who had volunteered himself as a hostage to secure his crew's freedom, was later freed by Navy SEAL forces on Sunday. Operating from the nearby USS Bainbridge, a guided-missile destroyer, the SEALs killed three pirates and successfully extracted Phillips. The remaining pirate was taken into custody.

"I feel great they got killed," Reza said. "I am happy." He expressed pride in the Navy's actions.

Phillips reached Mombasa, Kenya aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday, while the rest of the crew touched down at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland during the previous night.

Rios praised his captain's conduct: "Outstanding; he's extraordinary; he's [a] very brave man." Crewmate John White simply noted they felt "damn lucky to be alive."

Both Rios and Reza called for increased maritime security measures. "Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth," Rios urged. "All the countries got to get involved with this." Reza agreed, stating: "I think government should get involved. They should think about our safety, yes... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger."

*CNN's Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.*

# The Maersk Alabama Hijacking: Crew Members Recount Terrifying Encounter with Somali Pirates

Crew members aboard the Maersk Alabama have come forward to share their harrowing account of survival after their vessel came under siege by Somali pirates in one of the most dramatic maritime hijacking incidents in recent memory. The sailors described a chaotic and life-threatening confrontation in which armed attackers repeatedly fired AK-47 rifles and pointed weapons directly at crew members, creating an atmosphere of sheer terror aboard the U.S.-flagged cargo ship.

## Multiple Attempts Before the Breach

According to crew testimonies, the pirates did not succeed on their first attempt to seize the vessel. In fact, the assailants made three separate failed attempts to board the Maersk Alabama before finally breaching the ship's defenses on their fourth try. This persistence struck crew member William Rios as particularly telling—he became convinced that the attack was not the work of a single disorganized group, but rather involved coordination between different pirate factions working in tandem to overcome the ship's resistance.

## Emergency Protocols Under Fire

The assault began without warning, as the crew was suddenly confronted by the sound of gunfire mixed with the blaring of the ship's emergency alarms. In that critical moment, the crew sprang into action, relying on emergency training procedures they had rehearsed for exactly this kind of scenario. However, when pressed for specifics about what these procedures entailed, Rios remained deliberately vague, explaining that he did not want to risk providing a blueprint that could be used by future pirates seeking to hijack other vessels. His reticence underscored the ongoing threat that maritime piracy continues to pose to commercial shipping routes.

## A Bold Gambit Rooted in Shared Faith

The pirates' ultimate objective was clear: they intended to hold the ship and its crew hostage in exchange for a ransom demand of $3 million. However, the tables began to turn when crew member Zahid Reza, working alongside the ship's chief engineer, devised a daring plan to capture one of the attackers. The pirate in question, a young man named Abdul, became the target of this scheme. Reza recognized an opportunity in their shared Muslim faith, using this common ground to slowly build a rapport with Abdul and earn his trust—trust that would ultimately become the young pirate's undoing.

## The Ambush in the Engine Room

With Abdul's guard lowered, Reza and the chief engineer lured him into the ship's engine room, an area shrouded in darkness that provided the perfect setting for their ambush. Once inside, the chief engineer made his move, tackling Abdul to gain control of the situation. Reza then took action, stabbing the young pirate in the ensuing struggle. In the heat of the moment, Reza's instinct was to finish the job and kill Abdul outright, but the chief engineer intervened, insisting that they needed to keep the pirate alive—a decision that would prove crucial in the events that followed, as a living hostage held far more strategic value than a dead one in the tense standoff that was unfolding aboard the besieged vessel.

# Oxon Hill, Maryland

Oxon Hill is an unincorporated community located in Prince George's County, Maryland, situated along the eastern bank of the Potomac River just south of Washington, D.C. The area combines suburban residential neighborhoods with significant commercial and recreational attractions, making it a notable part of the greater Washington metropolitan region.

## History

The name "Oxon Hill" derives from the region's colonial-era history, with roots tracing back to English settlement patterns in the Chesapeake Bay area. The area was historically part of larger plantation lands during the colonial and antebellum periods, benefiting from its strategic location along the Potomac River, which facilitated trade and transportation.

## Geography and Location

Oxon Hill's proximity to Washington, D.C. has shaped its development as a bedroom community for the nation's capital. The community lies near the Woodrow Wilson Bridge, which connects Maryland to Virginia across the Potomac River, making it a significant transportation corridor. This strategic positioning has contributed to steady population growth and commercial development over the decades.

## Notable Features

The community is perhaps best known for hosting the **MGM National Harbor**, a major casino and resort complex that opened in 2016 near National Harbor, though National Harbor itself is technically a separate planned community. Oxon Hill also features:

- **Oxon Hill Farm** (part of the National Park Service's National Capital Parks-East), which preserves agricultural heritage and offers educational programming about 19th and 20th-century farming practices
- **Oxon Cove Park**, providing green space and recreational opportunities along the waterfront
- Proximity to National Harbor, a mixed-use development featuring hotels, restaurants, retail, and the Capital Wheel observation wheel

## Demographics and Community

As a diverse suburban area, Oxon Hill reflects the broader demographic makeup of Prince George's County, which has one of the highest concentrations of African American residents among counties in the United States. The community includes a mix of housing types, from single-family homes to apartment complexes, serving commuters who work in Washington, D.C., and the surrounding metropolitan area.

## Economic Significance

The presence of major attractions like MGM National Harbor has transformed the local economy, bringing jobs, tourism revenue, and increased development interest to the area. This has been part of a broader revitalization effort along the Potomac waterfront in this section of Prince George's County.

Oxon Hill continues to evolve as both a residential community and a destination, balancing its historical roots with modern suburban and commercial growth.

**Crew of Maersk Alabama Returns Home to Heroes' Welcome, Recounts Harrowing Ordeal**

*By CNN Staff*

NORFOLK, Virginia -- The crew of the Maersk Alabama arrived back on American soil this week to an emotional reception of family embraces, American flags, and news cameras eager to capture their first public accounts of the pirate attack that captured the world's attention.

The 20 crew members, who had been at sea for weeks following the April hijacking attempt off the coast of Somalia, described a terrifying ordeal that began as a routine morning and escalated within minutes into a fight for their lives.

"We saw them coming up fast behind us in that little skiff, and everybody just went into action," said Chief Engineer Mike Perry, who sustained injuries during the confrontation. "We'd drilled for this, but drilling and living it are two completely different things."

Crew members described how four armed pirates boarded the vessel, and the ship's crew, trained in anti-piracy procedures, worked to disable the engine room and secure themselves as Captain Richard Phillips remained on the bridge attempting to negotiate and protect his men.

"Captain Phillips gave himself up to protect us. There's no other way to say it," said Second Mate Ken Quinn, his voice breaking during a press conference at the pier. "He looked out for this crew like we were his own family."

The crew recounted a chaotic struggle in the ship's darkened engine room, where they briefly captured one of the pirates and attempted to use him as a bargaining chip to secure the captain's release. Phillips was ultimately taken hostage in one of the ship's lifeboats, beginning a five-day standoff at sea that ended when Navy SEAL snipers, acting on orders from the White House, killed three of the pirates and freed him.

"Those five days waiting to hear if he was okay -- that was the hardest part," said crew member ATM Reza. "We just kept thinking about his family, about our families back home worrying about all of us."

Many of the sailors expressed relief mixed with lingering unease, noting that the attack has changed how they think about their profession.

"You go into this job knowing there's risk, but you don't think it's going to be you," said Third Mate Colin Wright. "Now every one of us is going to look at these waters differently."

Family members who gathered at the dock described anxious days spent glued to television screens and phones, waiting for updates.

"When I saw him walk down that gangway, I just broke down," said Perry's wife, Seana. "You don't know how strong you are until something like this happens to someone you love."

Maersk Line Limited, the company that operates the vessel, has said it will conduct a full review of the incident and reevaluate security protocols for ships traveling through pirate-infested waters near the Horn of Africa, a region that has seen a dramatic rise in hijackings in recent years.

For now, though, the crew members say they are simply grateful to be reunited with loved ones.

"Every single day since this happened, I've thought about how lucky we are," Quinn said. "Not everybody comes home from something like this. We did, and we owe that to each other -- and to our captain."

Phillips, who was flown separately to meet with military officials following his rescue, is expected to reunite with his family in Vermont in the coming days. The crew said they hope to see him again soon, calling him not just their captain, but a friend forged through crisis.

"There's a bond now that nothing can break," Perry said. "We went through hell together, and we came out the other side."

# The Rescue of Captain Phillips: A Crew's Ordeal at Sea

## A Four-Day Crisis Ends in the Indian Ocean

In April 2009, the cargo ship Maersk Alabama became the center of an international drama after Somali pirates boarded the vessel approximately 240 nautical miles southeast of Eyl, Somalia. What followed was a tense standoff that captured global attention and tested the resolve of both a merchant crew and U.S. military forces.

## The Attack and Crew's Resistance

When four armed pirates boarded the Maersk Alabama on April 8, the ship's 20-member crew took extraordinary measures to protect themselves. Following established security protocols, most crew members locked themselves in the ship's engine room—a citadel of sorts—cutting off the vessel's power and steering capabilities. This left the pirates with limited control over the massive container ship.

Captain Richard Phillips made the pivotal decision to offer himself as a hostage in exchange for his crew's safety, a choice that would place him at the center of the unfolding crisis. The pirates, realizing they had lost control of the ship itself, took Phillips and fled in one of the Alabama's enclosed lifeboats, beginning a tense standoff on the open water.

## Crew Members Take Matters Into Their Own Hands

During the initial confrontation, crew members reportedly attempted their own countermeasures against the hijackers. Some accounts indicate that crew members briefly captured one of the pirates during the chaos, attempting to negotiate an exchange for their captain—though this effort did not ultimately secure Phillips' release.

The crew's actions throughout the ordeal demonstrated remarkable composure under extreme duress, as they worked to regain control of their vessel while their captain remained in the hands of armed captors nearby.

## Naval Intervention and the SEAL Operation

The USS Bainbridge, a Navy destroyer, arrived on the scene to monitor the situation as the lifeboat drifted with its hostage and captors aboard. Negotiations stretched on for days, with tensions mounting as fuel and supplies dwindled in the small vessel.

On April 12, the standoff reached its dramatic conclusion. Navy SEAL snipers, operating from the deck of the Bainbridge under cover of darkness, fired three precise shots that killed three of the pirates holding Phillips. A fourth pirate, who had boarded the Bainbridge earlier for medical treatment or negotiations, was taken into custody.

## Reactions to the Rescue

News of Phillips' safe rescue triggered immediate relief and celebration among the Maersk Alabama crew, who had endured days of uncertainty about their captain's fate. The successful operation was hailed as a demonstration of the precision and capability of U.S. special operations forces, executed in extremely challenging conditions—firing at a moving target from one vessel to another in low light.

Crew members and maritime officials praised both Phillips' selfless decision to protect his crew and the skill of the Navy personnel who orchestrated his rescue. The incident sparked renewed international attention on the growing threat of piracy off the Somali coast and led to increased naval patrols and security measures for commercial vessels transiting the region.

**OXON HILL, Maryland** — Survivors of a merchant vessel hijacking off the coast of Somalia gathered here this week to share harrowing accounts of their ordeal, renewing calls for expanded international naval patrols and stricter security protocols in one of the world's most dangerous shipping corridors.

Speaking at a maritime safety conference, crew members described the moment armed pirates boarded their cargo ship in the Gulf of Aden, an area that has long been plagued by piracy despite years of international efforts to secure the waters.

"We saw the skiffs approaching fast, and within minutes they were alongside us with ladders and weapons," said one crew member, who asked not to be identified by name citing concerns for his family's safety. "There was nothing we could do. We were unarmed, and they had automatic rifles."

The crew, comprised of nationals from several countries, said they were held for days as negotiations for their release played out. They described cramped conditions, psychological strain, and uncertainty about whether they would return home safely.

"Every hour felt like a lifetime," another survivor said. "You don't know if today is the day something goes wrong."

## Calls for Action

The testimonies come amid renewed concern among shipping industry officials that piracy in the region, while reduced from its peak roughly a decade ago, remains a persistent threat to commercial vessels navigating the narrow waters near the Horn of Africa.

Maritime security experts at the conference argued that current international naval deployments, while helpful, are insufficient to cover the vast expanse of ocean where attacks can occur.

"We need more coordinated patrols, faster response times, and better information-sharing between shipping companies and naval forces," said one industry representative in attendance. "Crews are the ones paying the price when security gaps are exploited."

Advocacy groups representing merchant mariners echoed those demands, pushing for:

- Increased funding for multinational naval task forces operating in the region
- Mandatory armed security teams aboard vessels transiting high-risk zones
- Enhanced early-warning systems to detect approaching skiffs
- Greater psychological support resources for crews who survive hijackings

## A Broader Pattern

Piracy off Somalia surged in the mid-2000s before international naval coalitions helped curb attacks through increased patrols and onboard security measures. However, officials note that instability in the region, combined with economic desperation among coastal communities, continues to create conditions ripe for renewed criminal activity at sea.

Shipping companies have increasingly relied on private armed guards and rerouting strategies, but crew advocates say these measures are inconsistently applied and leave gaps that pirates continue to exploit.

For the sailors who spoke in Oxon Hill, the message was less about policy details and more about basic survival.

"We just want to go to work and come home to our families," one crew member said. "That shouldn't be too much to ask."

Organizers of the conference said they plan to compile the testimonies into a formal report to present to maritime regulatory bodies and shipping industry leaders in the coming months.
